candidates.label: Promontory Palace, Caesarea Maritima
candidates.support: The Historical Marker Database records the location of the physical "Promontory Palace" marker, placed at the excavated site in the Caesarea Maritima National Park, as "32° 29.796′ N, 34° 53.402′ E"; this is corroborated by OpenStreetMap's independently drawn outline for the Promontory Palace (way 96066573, centred about 60 m away) and lies close to Wikidata's points for the adjacent Theater of Herod and Caesarea Hippodrome, which the marker's own text says the palace overlooks. Cornell University's archaeology program, which has worked at the site, describes a palace built around a large rock-cut pool on a rocky promontory extending about 100 meters into the sea, matching the first-century Jewish historian Josephus's account of a palace Herod the Great built at Caesarea; a peer-reviewed article in the Journal of Roman Archaeology, titled "The promontory palace at Caesarea Maritima: preliminary evidence for Herod's Praetorium," documents this identification in the scholarly literature. Wikidata's own point for "Herod's Palace" (Q2527367), by contrast, falls about 630 m north, nearer the harbor and Crusader-period town, and is not used here.

summary.text: Herod's palace at Caesarea was a seaside palace that Herod the Great built on a rocky promontory jutting into the Mediterranean, later excavated and identified as the "Promontory Palace." According to Acts, after Paul was brought to Caesarea under guard, the governor Felix ordered him kept in custody in Herod's palace to await his accusers.

history.text: Cornell University's archaeology program describes the Promontory Palace in two parts: a Lower Palace near sea level, with a colonnade framing a great rock-cut pool, and an Upper Palace on higher ground centered on a large paved courtyard, citing the first-century Jewish historian Josephus's account that Herod the Great built a splendid palace as a showpiece of his new city.

Acts records that when the Roman governor Felix learned Paul was from Cilicia, he said, "I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive," and ordered him kept under guard in Herod's palace; Paul remained in custody for two years, until Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus.

scripture.textWEB: “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
